transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well… I came in because I’ve been having a hard time not focusing on how I look, I guess, especially since I started helping with the safety trainings at work. I’m a production worker, and lately I’ve been helping point things out during the trainings, like showing people equipment or where to look, and when I see my hands out there, I just can’t stop noticing how wrinkly they look, and kind of uneven. Like one hand looks worse than the other, or the skin looks loose, and then I start worrying that everyone else is seeing it too while I’m talking.

And then it kind of carries over. We had some newsletter photos taken, and when I saw my face in them, I kept thinking it looked crooked or off somehow. Other people told me they didn’t see what I was talking about, but I still kept staring at it and thinking, “No, it’s there.” It’s been bothering me enough that I thought maybe I should talk to someone, because I don’t seem to be able to just let it go.
Have you found yourself avoiding situations, like speaking during trainings or being in photos, because you’re worried about how you look?

Yes… I mean, not completely. I’m still going to work, and I haven’t quit helping with the trainings or anything like that. I do still stand up there and point things out when I’m supposed to. But I notice I’m… fussier beforehand, I guess. Like I take longer getting ready, checking my hands, trying to decide if they look worse under certain lighting, or whether I should hold my papers a certain way so people aren’t looking right at them. It slows me down more than I’d like to admit.

And with photos, yes, I’ve started sort of stepping out of the way if I can. If someone says, “Let’s get a picture,” I might suddenly act like I need to go refill my coffee or help with something in the back. I don’t always make a big scene about it, but I’m definitely avoiding it more.

Social things too, a little. I still go, but I hesitate more than I used to. I’ll think about whether people are going to notice my face looking uneven or my hands looking old, and then something I used to just enjoy becomes this whole decision in my head. So it hasn’t stopped my life exactly, but it’s made things slower and less easy.

Do these concerns about your appearance ever become so bothersome that you have trouble focusing on anything else, or do they interfere with your ability to enjoy your day, even when you're not in photos or giving trainings?

Yes… it does, though I feel a little embarrassed saying that because it sounds so small when I put it into words. It’s not like anything dramatic is happening, but once I notice it, it kind of stays with me.

Like since I started helping with those safety trainings, I’ll be pointing at something or showing someone where to look, and then instead of just thinking about what I’m supposed to be explaining, I’m suddenly noticing my hands. The wrinkles, the way the skin looks loose, how one hand looks different from the other. And then I start wondering if everyone else can see it too, even if nobody says anything. It can keep running in the back of my mind afterward, not just during the training.

And with the newsletter pictures, that’s been the same kind of thing. I saw my face and thought it looked crooked or uneven somehow, and even though people told me they didn’t notice it, I kept going back to it in my head. I’ll be trying to enjoy the rest of the day, but part of me is still thinking about that picture or how I must have looked. So yes, it can make it hard to really settle into my day, because my mind keeps circling back to it.

Do you find yourself doing things over and over again, like checking your appearance in mirrors, taking a lot of time to get ready, or trying to fix or hide what you’re worried about, as a way to cope with these thoughts?

Yes… I do. More than I’d like, honestly. Before I have to be in front of people, like before one of the safety classes at work or even a workshop at the senior center, I’ll go into the bathroom and check the mirror, then I’ll leave, and then I’ll think, “Wait, maybe it looked different from that angle,” and I’ll go back and check again.

It’s usually my hands and my face. I’ll put lotion on my hands because I think maybe if they look less dry or wrinkled it won’t be so noticeable. And with my face, I’ll turn my head different ways in the mirror, like looking from one side and then the other, trying to see if it looks uneven. Sometimes I know I’m taking too long, but I still feel like I have to do it or I’ll be distracted the whole time.

And I’ve asked a coworker, too, which is embarrassing. I’ll say something like, “Do I look all right?” or “Does my face look strange?” I try to make it sound casual, like I’m just checking before going in front of a group, but really I’m looking for reassurance. It can make me run a little behind, not terribly late usually, but enough that I’m rushing afterward. I still get myself there and do what I’m supposed to do, but there’s this whole routine beforehand that I don’t feel good about.

When you look in the mirror and notice these things about your hands or your face, do you feel like you're seeing something that's very noticeable to others, even if they say they don’t see it, or do you feel like you're focusing on something very small that most people wouldn't really pay attention to?

I think… I think in the moment it feels very noticeable. That’s the part that’s hard to explain, because if I step back, I can sort of hear how other people might say, “Nobody is looking that closely.” But when I’m actually looking in the mirror, or when I’m up there helping with the safety trainings and I’m pointing something out, my eyes go right to my hands. They look so wrinkly to me, and uneven somehow, like one looks older or worse than the other, and then I imagine everybody else seeing exactly what I’m seeing.

And with my face, it’s similar. Especially after those newsletter photos, I saw the picture and I just thought, “My face looks crooked.” Other people have said they don’t see it, or they’ll say it looks fine, but I don’t know… I still see it. It doesn’t feel like a tiny thing when I’m looking at it. It feels obvious to me.

I can admit there’s a part of me that wonders if maybe I’m focusing on it more than other people would. I mean, nobody has actually come up and said anything about my hands or my face. But it doesn’t calm me down much, because once I notice it, it feels like it must be noticeable. Like if I can see it so clearly, I have trouble believing other people can’t.
Do you ever feel so distressed about these appearance concerns that it affects your ability to enjoy activities you used to like, or causes you a lot of emotional discomfort even when you're alone?

Yes… I think it does, but not in a way where I’ve completely stopped doing things. I still go to work, and I still help with the trainings, and I still volunteer when I said I would. So part of me wants to say, “Well, it’s not that bad,” because I am functioning, you know?

But it does take something out of those things. Before trainings, I’m slower getting ready because I’m checking and fussing and trying to make sure I look all right, and then I get irritated with myself because I know I’m making myself run behind. And with things that are supposed to be nice, like social events or stuff at the senior center, I notice I hesitate more than I used to. I’ll think, “Do I really want to go?” when really it’s more that I don’t want to feel uncomfortable about how I look.

Photos are probably the clearest example. I’ve started trying to duck out of them when I can, or stand in the back, or offer to take the picture instead. I didn’t used to think about it that much. It’s embarrassing because these are ordinary things, but yes, it does make it harder to enjoy myself. Even if I’m alone afterward, I can sit there thinking about how I looked or whether people noticed, and it just puts a cloud over the rest of the day.

When you’re worried about how your hands or face look, do you believe that these are major flaws that would be clearly noticeable to others, or do you sometimes think that they might not be as obvious as you perceive them to be?

I think it goes back and forth, honestly. When I’m in the middle of it, it feels like a major flaw. Like when I’m helping with the safety trainings and I’m pointing at something, I suddenly notice my hands and they look so wrinkly and uneven to me that I feel like everyone must be seeing it too. It’s hard to believe they wouldn’t, because it feels so obvious from where I’m standing.

And then with my face, the newsletter photos really set me off. I saw them and thought my face looked crooked, and even when people said they didn’t see what I was talking about, I still kept looking at it and thinking, “No, it’s right there.” But then another part of me knows, or at least wonders, that maybe I’m seeing it more strongly than other people are. Nobody else seems as bothered by it as I am.

So I don’t know that I always believe it’s as huge as it feels, but in the moment it feels very noticeable. That’s why I came in, really — since I started doing those trainings, I can’t seem to stop noticing my hands, and then it kind of spread to my face in pictures.
Do you find yourself repeating certain behaviors, like checking your appearance or seeking reassurance, because you feel like you have to do them to reduce your distress about how you look?

Yes, I do. I mean, not all day long or anything, but before I have to be in front of people, it definitely happens. Like before one of the classes or a workshop at the senior center, I’ll go into the bathroom and check the mirror, and then I’ll think, “Okay, that’s enough,” but then I’ll go back and check again. Sometimes it’s my face, turning it a little one way and then the other, trying to see if it looks crooked or if it’s just the lighting. And with my hands, I’ll put lotion on them because I think maybe if they don’t look so dry or wrinkly, I won’t feel as self-conscious.

It sounds silly when I say it out loud, but in the moment it feels like I have to do it before I can go in and start. Like if I don’t check, I’ll be distracted the whole time. And sometimes I’ll ask a coworker something like, “Do I look okay?” or “Is my face looking weird in this light?” I try to say it casually, because I don’t want to seem like I’m fishing for compliments, but really I’m looking for them to tell me it’s fine.

It does calm me down a little, but only for a short time. And then I end up running a little behind because I’ve spent those extra minutes checking or putting lotion on again. But I still get myself there. I don’t usually cancel or anything. It just makes getting there more stressful than it probably needs to be.
